title: Malware
starter: A school laptop suddenly runs slowly, shows pop-ups and its files have odd names. Suggest three things that might have happened to it.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: What is malware?
facts: Malware is short for malicious software: any program written to damage or gain access to a system.
It can delete or change files, steal data, spy on users or take control of a computer.
It spreads through downloads, attachments, websites and USB sticks.
stations.challenge: Write a definition of malware in your own words.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Malware is short for malicious software: any program written to damage or gain access to a system.
Also credit: It can delete or change files, steal data, spy on users or take control of a computer.

questions.a: Malicious software: programs written to cause harm or gain access

questions.q: Which is the most common way malware reaches a computer?
questions.a: A user opens an infected email attachment or download

stations.name: Viruses
facts: A virus attaches itself to a file or program.
It needs the user to run that file before it can do anything.
Once running, it copies itself into other files and spreads when those files are shared.
stations.challenge: Why does a virus need a user to do something?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A virus attaches itself to a file or program.
Also credit: It needs the user to run that file before it can do anything.

questions.a: It attaches to files, and spreads when those files are opened and shared

questions.q: Which of these could carry a virus?
questions.a: A program file attached to an email

stations.name: Worms
facts: A worm is self-replicating: it copies itself without any user action.
It spreads across networks by finding weaknesses in software.
Worms can spread extremely fast and use up bandwidth and processing time.
stations.challenge: Why can a worm spread faster than a virus?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A worm is self-replicating: it copies itself without any user action.
Also credit: It spreads across networks by finding weaknesses in software.

questions.q: What makes a worm different from a virus?
questions.a: A worm copies itself across a network without any user action

questions.q: Which defence helps most against worms?
questions.a: Keeping software and operating systems patched and up to date

stations.name: Trojans
facts: A trojan is disguised as legitimate software, such as a free game or a useful tool.
The user installs it themselves, and it then does something harmful.
Trojans don't replicate, but they often open a backdoor for the attacker.
stations.challenge: Why is the trojan named after the wooden horse?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A trojan is disguised as legitimate software, such as a free game or a useful tool.
Also credit: The user installs it themselves, and it then does something harmful.

questions.a: Malware disguised as legitimate software that the user installs themselves

questions.q: What does a backdoor let an attacker do?
questions.a: Access the computer again later, without the normal login

stations.name: Ransomware and spyware
facts: Ransomware encrypts the user's files and demands a payment for the key.
Spyware secretly records what the user does, including keystrokes, and sends it to the attacker.
A keylogger is a common form of spyware used to capture passwords.
stations.challenge: Why are good backups the best defence against ransomware?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Ransomware encrypts the user's files and demands a payment for the key.
Also credit: Spyware secretly records what the user does, including keystrokes, and sends it to the attacker.

questions.a: Encrypts files and demands payment for the key to unlock them
Spyware that records every key pressed, including passwords

stations.name: Stopping malware
facts: Anti-malware software scans files and checks them against known threats.
Keep operating systems and applications patched and up to date.
Don't open unexpected attachments, and back up important files regularly.
Firewalls and user access levels limit what malware can reach.
stations.challenge: Suggest four things a school could do to reduce malware infections.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Anti-malware software scans files and checks them against known threats.
Also credit: Keep operating systems and applications patched and up to date.

questions.q: Which of these help protect against malware? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Anti-malware software kept up to date; Installing operating system updates; Regular backups; Not opening unexpected attachments

final.name: Final challenge: identify the malware

questions.q: Which type of malware does each description match?
questions.a: Attaches to a file and spreads when that file is shared = Virus; Copies itself across a network with no user action = Worm; Pretends to be a free game, then opens a backdoor = Trojan; Encrypts every document and demands Bitcoin = Ransomware; Needs the user to run an infected program = Virus; Exploits a weakness in unpatched software to spread by itself = Worm; Downloaded as a 'video player update' that steals passwords = Trojan; Displays a countdown and a payment demand = Ransomware

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Name two types of malware and state what each one does.
points: Malware is short for malicious software: any program written to damage or gain access to a system.
The user installs it themselves, and it then does something harmful.
Spyware secretly records what the user does, including keystrokes, and sends it to the attacker.
Firewalls and user access levels limit what malware can reach.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: Explain why a worm can spread through a network faster than a virus.
points: It spreads through downloads, attachments, websites and USB sticks.
A virus attaches itself to a file or program.
Worms can spread extremely fast and use up bandwidth and processing time.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Describe three measures a school could take to reduce malware infections.
points: Malware is short for malicious software: any program written to damage or gain access to a system.
Firewalls and user access levels limit what malware can reach.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 6.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
